decks.title: Broken Access Control
cards: Key terms

Broken access control: an app failing to check what a logged-in user is allowed to see or do.
Insecure direct object reference (IDOR): changing an ID in a request to see someone else's data, because the app doesn't check ownership.
Server-side request forgery (SSRF): tricking a server into fetching a URL for the attacker, often an internal one.
Cloud metadata service: a built-in cloud service that gives a server its settings and temporary credentials.
What it is

Broken access control means users can act outside their intended permissions. They might read other people's records, change someone else's account or reach admin pages. It's number one in OWASP Top 10:2025.
Real example

In 2019 First American Financial exposed about 885 million records. Its document links used sequential numbers with no ownership check. Change the number in the address and you saw someone else's documents.
SSRF is now part of A01
SSRF moved into A01 in 2025.
SSRF example: Capital One

At Capital One in 2019, an attacker used server-side request forgery (SSRF) against a cloud server. The server fetched its own credentials from the cloud metadata service and passed them to the attacker.
Prevent it: check every request
Deny by default. Check authorisation on the server for every request, including that the user owns the record. Never rely on hidden links or client-side checks.
Prevent SSRF

Allow-list outbound destinations, so the server only fetches approved addresses. Block requests to cloud metadata addresses. On Amazon Web Services (AWS), require Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2), which makes simple server-side request forgery (SSRF) far harder.

q.q: A user changes `/orders/1043` to `/orders/1044` and sees a stranger's order. What's missing?
o: A longer session timeout
A server-side ownership check
Stronger Transport Layer Security (TLS)
q.w: A server-side ownership check. This is an insecure direct object reference (IDOR), a classic A01 flaw. The server must check ownership on every request. Not TLS or a session timeout: neither stops a logged-in user asking for another record.

decks.title: Security Misconfiguration
cards: Key terms

Security misconfiguration: insecure settings, rather than buggy code, that leave a system open to attack.
Hardening: changing insecure default settings to shrink the attack surface.
Cloud security posture management (CSPM): a tool that scans cloud settings automatically for risky misconfigurations.
Stack trace: a detailed error report that lists the functions and file paths running when the error happened.
What it is

Security misconfiguration means insecure settings rather than buggy code. Examples include default passwords, unneeded features left on, verbose error pages, open cloud storage and missing security headers.
Why it rose to A02
Security misconfiguration rose to A02 in 2025. The reason is that modern apps are mostly configuration.
Real example
Researchers regularly find cloud storage buckets and databases left open to the internet with no password. These expose millions of records. Nobody hacked anything clever. A setting was simply wrong.
Prevent it: harden every build
Build every environment from the same hardened, repeatable configuration. Remove features and accounts you don't use.
Prevent it: scan cloud settings
Scan cloud settings automatically, for example with a cloud security posture management (CSPM) tool. Review them after every change.

q.q: A production web app shows full stack traces with file paths when it errors. Which category fits best?
o: A02 Security Misconfiguration
A05 Injection
A07 Authentication Failures
q.w: A02 Security Misconfiguration. Debug output left switched on in production is a configuration mistake. It also touches A10, which covers error handling. Either way, it shows attackers how your code is laid out. Not A05 or A07: no input runs as code, and no login is involved.

decks.title: Software Supply Chain Failures
cards: Key terms

Software supply chain: everything that goes into your software, such as libraries, build tools, pipelines and the people who maintain them.
Software bill of materials (SBOM): a list of every component and version in the software you ship.
Continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) pipeline: automated steps that build, test and release code.
Backdoor: hidden code that gives an attacker secret access.
What it is

Software Supply Chain Failures is new in 2025. It expands 2021's Vulnerable and Outdated Components to the whole supply chain. That includes the libraries you depend on, build tools, continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) pipelines and the people who maintain them. You inherit their weaknesses.
Real example

In March 2024 an engineer noticed Secure Shell (SSH) logins were about half a second slow. They traced it to a backdoor in the xz compression library. A contributor had spent around two years earning maintainer trust before slipping it in. It was caught before most stable Linux releases shipped it.
Prevent it: know what you run
Keep a software bill of materials (SBOM), so you know what you run. Scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities and update promptly.
Prevent it: lock down the chain
Pin versions, so updates only arrive when you choose. Verify signatures and use trusted registries. Lock down who can change your build pipeline.

q.q: Which practice helps most to find out whether you're affected when a new library flaw is announced?
o: Making staff use longer passwords
Keeping a software bill of materials (SBOM)
Turning on multi-factor authentication (MFA)
q.w: Keeping an SBOM. It lists every component and version you ship, so you can answer “are we exposed?” in minutes instead of days. Not MFA or longer passwords: they protect logins, but they don't show which components you run.

decks.title: Cryptographic Failures
cards: Key terms

Hash: a short fingerprint of data that changes if the data changes.
Salt: a random value added to each password before hashing, so identical passwords get different hashes.
Key management service: a service that stores and controls encryption keys outside your code.
Secrets manager: a service that stores keys, passwords and other secrets safely, outside your code.
What it is

Cryptographic failures mean sensitive data isn't properly protected by cryptography. Data might be sent over plain Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) or stored unencrypted. It might be hashed with fast algorithms like MD5, or protected with weak or hard-coded keys.
Real example

In 2013 Adobe lost data on around 150 million accounts. The passwords were encrypted with one key in a weak mode instead of being hashed. So identical passwords produced identical results. Password hints sat beside them in plain text.
Prevent it: encrypt and hash
Use Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 or 1.3 everywhere. Encrypt sensitive data at rest, meaning while it's stored. Hash passwords with Argon2 or bcrypt.
Prevent it: protect your keys
Keep keys in a key management service, never in source code. Never invent your own encryption.

q.q: A developer stores application programming interface (API) keys in the app's source code on GitHub. What's the best fix?
o: Make the repository private
Base64-encode the keys in the code
Rotate them and use a secrets manager
q.w: Rotate the keys and use a secrets manager. Once a key has been committed, it's compromised, so rotate it, meaning replace it with a new key. A private repository leaves the old keys valid. Base64 is encoding, not protection.

decks.title: Injection
cards: Key terms

Injection: an attack where an app treats user input as code.
Cross-site scripting (XSS): injecting script into a web page so it runs in other users' browsers.
Parameterised query: a database query that keeps user input separate from the command.
Object-relational mapper (ORM): a library that builds database queries from code, so you don't write them by hand.
What it is

Injection happens when an app treats untrusted input as code or commands. Structured Query Language (SQL) injection, operating system (OS) command injection and cross-site scripting (XSS) all fall here. It's A05 in 2025.
Real example

In May 2023 the Cl0p gang exploited a SQL injection zero-day in MOVEit Transfer, a file-transfer product. A zero-day is a flaw attackers use before a fix exists. They stole data from thousands of organisations, affecting nearly 100 million people. This happened before most victims knew the flaw existed.
Prevent it: queries and input

Use parameterised queries or a safe object-relational mapper (ORM), never string-built SQL. Validate input against an allow-list. Give database accounts least privilege, meaning only the access they need.
Prevent XSS: encode output
Encode output for the context it lands in, such as HTML, JavaScript or URLs. Encoding stops the browser treating text as code, which stops cross-site scripting (XSS).

q.q: Which of these stops SQL injection most reliably?
o: Hiding error messages
Using parameterised queries
Using encrypted HTTPS connections
q.w: Using parameterised queries. They keep data separate from the query, so input can't change its meaning. Hiding errors only makes injection harder to spot. HTTPS encrypts traffic in transit, but doesn't change how the server treats input.

decks.title: Insecure Design
cards: Key terms

Insecure design: a flaw in how a feature was planned, not in how it was coded.
Threat modelling: thinking through what could go wrong with a feature, and who would abuse it, before you build it.
Abuse case: a description of how someone could misuse a feature, written next to the normal user story.
Rate limiting: capping how many requests someone can make in a set time.
What it is

Insecure design means flaws in the design itself, not in the code. A perfectly coded feature can still be unsafe if nobody thought about how it could be abused. Patching the code can't fix a bad design.
Example: security questions
A password reset that relies on security questions like “mother's maiden name” is insecure by design. The answers are often public.
Example: unlimited stock
A checkout is insecure by design if it lets one user reserve unlimited stock with no rate limit.
Prevent it: threat model first
Threat model new features before building them. Ask what could go wrong and who would abuse it. Write abuse cases next to user stories.
Prevent it: patterns and limits
Use proven secure design patterns. Build in limits, such as rate limiting and per-user caps.

q.q: What's the most effective time to catch an insecure design flaw?
o: During design, through threat modelling
After launch, through a penetration test
After an incident, in the review
q.w: During design, through threat modelling. Fixing a design on paper is cheap. Fixing it after launch can mean rebuilding the feature. A penetration test, which is a simulated attack, and an incident review only find the flaw once it's live.

decks.title: Authentication Failures
cards: Key terms

Authentication: checking proof that you are who you claim to be.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA): proving who you are with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password and a phone.
Passkey: a login stored on your device that only works on the real website it was created for.
Credential stuffing: trying username and password pairs leaked from other sites.
What it is

Authentication failures are weaknesses in proving who someone is. Examples include no multi-factor authentication (MFA), allowing weak or breached passwords and unlimited login attempts. Weak account recovery and sessions that never expire count too.
Real example

In February 2024 attackers used stolen credentials on a Change Healthcare remote access portal. The portal didn't require multi-factor authentication (MFA). The ransomware attack that followed disrupted claims processing across US healthcare for weeks. Ransomware is malware that locks or steals data and demands payment.
Prevent it: require strong MFA
Require multi-factor authentication (MFA), ideally phishing-resistant passkeys or FIDO2 keys. Phishing-resistant means they still protect you if you log in on a fake website.
Prevent it: guard every login
Block known breached passwords. Rate-limit and monitor login attempts. Expire sessions properly. Protect recovery flows as carefully as the login itself.

q.q: Which control would most directly have stopped the Change Healthcare login?
o: Disk encryption
MFA on the remote access portal
A web application firewall rule
q.w: MFA on the remote access portal. Stolen passwords alone were enough to log in, and a second factor would have blocked that first step. Not disk encryption or a firewall rule: neither stops someone logging in with valid credentials.

decks.title: Software or Data Integrity Failures
cards: Key terms

Digital signature: a cryptographic mark that proves who signed data and that it wasn't altered.
Code signing: signing software so users can check who made it and that it wasn't changed.
Deserialisation: turning stored or received data back into objects a program can use.
Continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) pipeline: automated steps that build, test and release code.
What it is

Software or data integrity failures mean trusting code or data without checking it hasn't been tampered with. Examples include updates installed without a signature check and plugins from untrusted sources. Another is untrusted data deserialised into objects.
Real example

The SolarWinds attack was discovered in December 2020. Malicious code was inserted during the build, so the poisoned Orion updates were properly signed. Customers' integrity checks passed because the build itself had been compromised.
Prevent it: check signatures
Verify digital signatures on updates and packages. Protect the continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) pipeline with access controls, reviews and logging.
Prevent unsafe deserialisation
Don't deserialise untrusted data. If you must accept it, use formats like JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) with strict validation instead.

q.q: An app runs updates downloaded over plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), with no signature check. What's the main risk?
o: The update downloads slowly
An attacker swaps the update
Users get locked out of the app
q.w: An attacker swaps the update. An on-path attacker sits between the app and the server, and the app runs whatever arrives. Slow downloads and lockouts aren't the risk.

decks.title: Security Logging and Alerting Failures
cards: Key terms

Log: a record of events, such as logins and errors, that a system writes as it runs.
Alert: a message that tells a person something suspicious has happened.
Security information and event management (SIEM): a system that collects logs from many systems in one place, correlates them and raises alerts.
Incident response: the plan and steps for detecting, containing and recovering from a security incident.
What it is
Security logging and alerting failures mean not logging security events, not alerting on them, or not acting on the alerts.
Why the name changed
Its 2025 name is Security Logging and Alerting Failures. In 2021 it was Security Logging and Monitoring Failures. "Alerting" replaced "Monitoring" because logs nobody acts on don't stop anything.
Real example
During the 2013 Target breach, security tools raised alerts as the attackers set up their malware. The alerts weren't acted on in time, and about 40 million card numbers were stolen.
Prevent it: log the right events
Log logins, failures, access-control denials and admin actions with enough context. Send logs to a central security information and event management (SIEM) system. Protect logs from tampering.
Prevent it: make alerts count
Alert on suspicious patterns. Test that alerts reach a person. Have an incident response plan.

q.q: Your app logs failed logins, but nobody reviews them and nothing alerts. Which category is this?
o: A02 Security Misconfiguration
A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures
A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
q.w: A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures. Logs only help if someone is alerted and acts. Not A02 or A10: nothing is misconfigured and no error is mishandled. The gap is alerting.

decks.title: Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
cards: Key terms

Exceptional condition: an error or unusual situation, such as bad input or a failed connection.
Failing open: allowing access when a security check breaks.
Failing closed: denying access when a security check breaks.
Out-of-bounds memory read: a program reading memory outside the area it's allowed to use.
What it is

Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions is new in 2025. It covers apps that handle errors and unusual conditions badly. Examples include failing open, crashing on unexpected input, leaking details in error messages, or leaving a transaction half-finished.
Real example

On 19 July 2024 a faulty CrowdStrike content update triggered an out-of-bounds memory read. The Falcon sensor didn't handle it, and about 8.5 million Windows computers crashed. It wasn't an attack, but airlines, banks and hospitals went down.
Prevent it: fail closed
Fail closed: when something goes wrong, deny access rather than allow it.
Prevent it: handle errors
Catch and handle errors. Show users generic messages while logging the details.
Prevent it: test and stage
Test edge cases and bad input. Roll out changes in stages, so a bad update reaches only a few systems first.

q.q: A login check throws an error when the database is slow, and the code then lets the user in. What's the flaw?
o: The code fails open
The site lacks HTTPS encryption
Password hashing is weak
q.w: The code fails open. When a security check can't complete, the safe default is to deny. Failing open turns an outage into a breach. Not weak hashing or missing HTTPS encryption: the user got in because the check errored.

decks.title: Change Healthcare
cards: Key terms

Ransomware: malware that locks or steals data and demands payment.
Credentials: the details you log in with, such as a username and password.
Remote access portal: a login page that lets people reach internal systems from outside the network.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA): proving who you are with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password and a phone.
What happened

In February 2024, the ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware gang attacked Change Healthcare, which processes a huge share of US medical claims. Its systems went offline, which disrupted claims and payments for pharmacies and providers for weeks.
How they got in

Attackers logged in to a Citrix remote access portal with stolen credentials. The portal didn't require multi-factor authentication (MFA). From there they moved through the network, stole data and deployed ransomware.
Impact
The company paid a US$22 million ransom. In July 2025 it told the US health regulator that about 192.7 million people were affected. That is the largest healthcare data breach on record in the US.
Lesson: MFA on every portal
Every remote access portal needs MFA, with no exceptions for old systems. At Change Healthcare, stolen credentials alone were enough to get in.
Lesson: paying isn't the end
Paying a ransom didn't make the problem go away. Data from the same attack was later used in further extortion attempts.
decks.maps: A07 Authentication Failures · MFA on remote access

q.q: What was the single missing control at Change Healthcare's entry point?
o: MFA on the Citrix portal
Encryption of the claims database
An antivirus update
q.w: MFA on the Citrix portal. Attackers logged in with stolen credentials, and no second factor stopped them. Not database encryption: the attackers came in as a valid user. Not an antivirus update: they needed no exploit, just a valid login.

decks.entry: Stolen credentials on a Citrix remote access portal with no MFA.
decks.impact: Claims processing across the US was disrupted for weeks. A US$22 million ransom was paid, and about 192.7 million people were affected.
decks.lesson: Every remote access portal needs MFA, with no exceptions for old systems.

attack: T1555.003 Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
decks.title: Medibank
cards: Key terms

Credentials: the details you log in with, such as a username and password.
Infostealer: malware that steals saved passwords and login data from a computer.
Virtual private network (VPN): a secure link that lets staff log in to a work network remotely.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA): proving who you are with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password and a phone.
What happened

In October 2022, Australian health insurer Medibank found that attackers had stolen customer data. The data covered about 9.7 million current and former customers. It included health claims information.
How they got in

Infostealer malware stole credentials a contractor had saved in their browser. It ran on the personal computer of an IT service desk contractor. The attackers used those credentials to log in to Medibank's virtual private network (VPN). The VPN didn't require multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Impact

Medibank refused to pay the ransom. The attackers published customer data on the dark web, including sensitive health records. The dark web is a hidden part of the internet that you can only reach with special software, such as Tor. Australia later sanctioned a Russian national over it, banning dealings with his money and his entry.
Lesson: MFA everywhere
Contractor and admin accounts need MFA everywhere. With MFA, a stolen password alone usually isn't enough to log in.
Lesson: admin logins off home PCs
Don't let privileged credentials live on personal devices. Privileged credentials are logins with admin-level powers.
Lesson: plan for a leak
Refusing to pay a ransom is often the right choice. Plan for the data being published anyway.
decks.maps: A07 Authentication Failures · MFA and privileged access

q.q: How did the attackers first get Medibank credentials?
o: Malware on a contractor's PC
A SQL injection flaw
A stolen backup tape
q.w: Malware on a contractor's PC. It took logins saved in the browser, and the VPN had no MFA. Not SQL injection or a stolen tape: the attackers simply logged in.

decks.entry: Malware stole a contractor's saved login. The VPN had no MFA.
decks.impact: Data on about 9.7 million customers, including health claims, was stolen and published.
decks.lesson: Require MFA on the VPN and keep work credentials off personal computers.

decks.title: Waikato DHB
cards: Key terms

Ransomware: malware that locks or steals data and demands payment.
Data exfiltration: copying data out of a network without permission.
Double extortion: ransomware that steals data and then encrypts it, so attackers can threaten to leak it as well as lock it.
Segmentation: splitting a network into zones, with rules that limit traffic between them.
What happened

In May 2021, ransomware caused a full IT outage across the hospitals of Waikato District Health Board (DHB) in New Zealand. The DHB is now part of Te Whatu Ora. Staff went back to pen and paper. Many clinics and procedures were postponed.
How they got in
The full initial access details weren't published. The attackers had access long enough to steal data before encrypting systems. That shows the intrusion went unnoticed for a while.
Impact

Data exfiltration was confirmed, meaning attackers copied data out of the network. Patient and staff data was leaked. Core systems took weeks to recover, and full recovery took much longer. The ransom wasn't paid.
Lesson: backups and segments
Health systems need tested offline backups and network segmentation. Segmentation splits a network into zones, with rules that limit traffic between them.
Lesson: plan to work without IT
Health systems need an incident plan that includes working without IT. At Waikato, staff had to go back to pen and paper.
Lesson: detect before encryption
Detecting attackers before they encrypt gives you far more options. At Waikato, the attackers stole data before anyone noticed them.
decks.maps: Backups, segmentation and incident response

q.q: Waikato DHB confirmed data was stolen. What does that mean for recovery from backups?
o: Backups restore systems but can't undo the theft
Backups get the stolen data back from the attackers
Backups stop the stolen data from being leaked
q.w: Backups restore systems but can't undo the theft. Leaked data stays leaked. Not getting the data back: backups only copy your own systems. Not stopping a leak: the attackers already hold a copy.

decks.entry: Not published. Attackers stayed unnoticed long enough to steal data before encrypting.
decks.impact: A full IT outage across its hospitals. Patient and staff data was stolen and later posted online.
decks.lesson: Backups restore systems but don't undo data theft. Detect early and segment the network.
decks.source: Waikato DHB and Te Whatu Ora, 2021 to 2022

decks.title: Latitude Financial
cards: Key terms

Credentials: the details you log in with, such as a username and password.
Third-party access: access to your systems or data held by an outside company, such as a vendor.
Data retention: how long an organisation keeps data before deleting it.
What happened

In March 2023, Latitude Financial disclosed a cyberattack. Latitude is a lender in Australia and New Zealand. About 14 million customer records were stolen. They included around 7.9 million driver licence numbers.
How they got in
The attack came in through a major vendor. It gave the attackers a Latitude employee's login credentials. They used those credentials to reach customer data held by two service providers.
Impact
Some records went back to 2005, long after customers had left. Latitude refused to pay the ransom. Regulators in both countries investigated.
Lesson: keep data only as needed
Keep data only as long as you need it. Data you deleted years ago can't be stolen.
Lesson: watch vendor access
Monitor vendor and third-party access closely. At Latitude, the attack came in through a major vendor.
decks.maps: Third-party risk · data minimisation

q.q: Which lesson does Latitude show most clearly?
o: Delete customer data you no longer need
Pay the ransom to protect customers
Third parties rarely cause breaches
q.w: Delete customer data you no longer need. Millions of affected records belonged to former customers whose data could have been deleted. Not paying: Latitude refused, and paying wouldn't undo the theft. Not third parties: this attack came in through a vendor.

decks.entry: A Latitude employee's login credentials, obtained through a major vendor.
decks.impact: About 14 million records stolen, including around 7.9 million driver licence numbers.
decks.lesson: Delete data you no longer need. Records from 2005 shouldn't still be there.

decks.title: MOVEit Transfer
cards: Key terms

Injection: an attack where an app treats user input as code.
Zero-day: a flaw attackers use before a fix exists.
Web shell: a malicious script planted on a web server that lets an attacker run commands on it remotely.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE): an ID that names one publicly known vulnerability.
What happened

In May 2023, the Cl0p ransomware gang mass-exploited MOVEit Transfer. MOVEit Transfer is a file-transfer product used by governments, banks and universities. Cl0p stole files rather than encrypting systems.
How they got in

Cl0p exploited a zero-day (CVE-2023-34362) in the MOVEit web application. It was a Structured Query Language (SQL) injection flaw. It let them run their own code and plant a web shell on internet-facing servers.
Impact
About 2,700 organisations and nearly 100 million people were affected. Many were hit through suppliers they'd never heard of. Cl0p extorted victims by threatening to publish the data.
Lesson: patch file transfer fast
Internet-facing file-transfer tools are high-value targets. Patch them urgently.
Lesson: limit stored data
Limit what data sits on file-transfer tools, and for how long. Cl0p stole files, so less stored data means less to steal.
Lesson: know suppliers' tools
Know which of your suppliers use these tools. Many MOVEit victims were hit through suppliers they'd never heard of.
decks.maps: A05 Injection · patching and supplier risk

q.q: What type of flaw did Cl0p exploit in MOVEit Transfer?
o: SQL injection
A weak password
A misconfigured firewall
q.w: SQL injection. It was a zero-day in the web application, so no patch existed when the attacks began. Not a weak password or a firewall: Cl0p exploited a flaw in the code, not a login or a setting.

decks.entry: A SQL injection zero-day (CVE-2023-34362) in the MOVEit Transfer web app.
decks.impact: About 2,700 organisations and nearly 100 million people were affected, many through their suppliers.
decks.lesson: Patch internet-facing file transfer tools fast and know which suppliers hold your data.

decks.title: Log4Shell
cards: Key terms

Log: a record of events, such as logins and errors, that a system writes as it runs.
Library: ready-made code that many programs reuse instead of writing it themselves.
Dependency: a library or other software that your software needs in order to run.
Software bill of materials (SBOM): a list of every component and version in the software you ship.
What happened

In December 2021, a critical flaw was disclosed in Log4j. Log4j is a logging library inside a huge number of Java applications. The flaw's Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) ID is CVE-2021-44228. It scored the maximum 10.0 severity.
How it worked

If an app logged a string an attacker controlled, Log4j could follow a lookup in that string and load remote code. The string could be a username or a browser header. Simply getting text into a log was enough.
Impact
Attackers began scanning for it within hours. Many organisations didn't know where they used Log4j. It was buried inside other products and libraries.
Lesson: know your dependencies
Know your dependencies, including the ones inside other software. Log4j was often a dependency of a dependency.
Lesson: keep an SBOM
Keep a software bill of materials (SBOM), a list of every component and version you ship. With an SBOM and fast patching, finding a buried library becomes a routine check.
decks.maps: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures · SBOM

q.q: Why was Log4Shell so hard for many organisations to respond to?
o: They didn't know which systems had Log4j
The fix took many months to be released
It mainly affected Windows servers
q.w: They didn't know which systems had Log4j. It was often a dependency of a dependency, so teams hunted for it system by system. Not the fix: the hard part was finding where to apply it. Not Windows: Log4j was in Java apps on many systems.

decks.entry: Attacker-controlled text written to a log made Log4j load remote code (CVE-2021-44228).
decks.impact: A 10.0 severity flaw in countless Java apps, scanned for within hours of disclosure.
decks.lesson: Keep a software bill of materials (SBOM) so you can find a buried library in minutes.

attack: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
decks.title: The xz utils backdoor
cards: Key terms

Backdoor: hidden code that gives an attacker secret access.
Secure Shell (SSH): an encrypted protocol for logging in to and managing remote machines.
Maintainer: a person who looks after an open-source project and approves changes to it.
Rolling release: a way of releasing software that ships updates continuously, instead of in fixed versions.
What happened

In March 2024, Microsoft engineer Andres Freund noticed something odd on a test system. Secure Shell (SSH) logins used more processing power (CPU) and took about half a second longer. He traced it to a backdoor in xz utils versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1.
How it got in

A contributor known as “Jia Tan” spent around two years building trust in the project. They became a maintainer. The malicious code was hidden in test files and build scripts, not in the visible source.
Impact

The backdoor targeted SSH on some Linux distributions. It was caught while mostly in testing and rolling releases, before most stable systems. Kali, a rolling release, briefly shipped it in late March 2024. It could have given someone remote access to many servers.
Lesson: maintainers are few
Open-source projects often rest on a few unpaid maintainers. One trusted contributor can change code that runs on many systems.
Lesson: notice odd behaviour
Watch for unexpected behaviour. About half a second of extra login time exposed this backdoor.
Lesson: check what you ship
Check what's in release packages. Treat build pipelines as part of your attack surface, meaning all the ways an attacker could get in. The xz payload hid in test files and build scripts.
decks.maps: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures

q.q: How was the xz backdoor discovered?
o: An engineer looked into slow SSH logins
An antivirus tool flagged the build files
A code reviewer spotted it in the source
q.w: An engineer looked into slow SSH logins. Curiosity about a small performance change caught one of the most serious supply chain attacks yet. Not antivirus or code review: the payload hid in test files and build scripts, not the visible source.

decks.entry: A trusted maintainer of about two years hid a backdoor in xz utils build files.
decks.impact: Caught mostly in testing and rolling releases, before most stable Linux systems shipped it.
decks.lesson: Open source often rests on a few maintainers. Pin versions; watch for odd changes.

decks.title: CrowdStrike outage
cards: Key terms

Kernel driver: low-level software that runs inside the core of the operating system, with full control of the machine.
Out-of-bounds memory read: a program reading memory outside the area it's allowed to use.
Staged rollout: releasing an update to a small group first, then to everyone if nothing breaks.
BitLocker recovery key: a long code that unlocks a BitLocker-encrypted Windows drive when Windows can't unlock it itself.
What happened
On 19 July 2024, a faulty content update for CrowdStrike's Falcon sensor crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers. They got stuck on a blue screen at boot.
What went wrong
It wasn't an attack. The update contained data the sensor's code didn't expect. That caused an out-of-bounds memory read inside a kernel driver. The error wasn't handled, so Windows crashed.
Impact
Airlines grounded flights. Hospitals, banks and broadcasters were disrupted around the world. Many machines needed hands-on fixes, one at a time, often with BitLocker recovery keys.
Lesson: test unexpected input
Test updates against unexpected input, and handle errors safely. Here, one unhandled error crashed millions of machines.
Lesson: roll out in stages
Roll updates out in stages. A staged rollout releases to a small group first, so a bad update hits fewer machines.
Lesson: reachable recovery keys
Keep BitLocker recovery keys somewhere you can reach when Windows won't boot. Many machines needed them to recover.
decks.maps: A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions · staged rollouts

q.q: Which OWASP Top 10:2025 category fits this crash best?
o: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures
A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures
A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
q.w: A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions. Unexpected input caused an unhandled error. A03 is the trap: the update came through a vendor, but the cause was bad input. Not A09: missing logs didn't cause the crash.

decks.entry: Not an attack. A faulty Falcon update crashed a Windows kernel driver.
decks.impact: About 8.5 million Windows PCs crashed, disrupting flights, hospitals and banks.
decks.lesson: Roll out updates in stages, and handle bad input without crashing.
decks.source: CrowdStrike root cause analysis and Microsoft, 2024

attack: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
decks.title: Uber
cards: Key terms

Multi-factor authentication (MFA): proving who you are with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password and a phone.
Push approval: a prompt on your phone that you tap to log in.
MFA fatigue: sending many MFA prompts until a tired or confused user approves one.
Secrets manager: a service that stores keys, passwords and other secrets safely, outside your code.
What happened
In September 2022, an attacker got broad access to Uber's internal systems. These included chat, cloud consoles and security tools. The attacker announced it in Uber's own Slack.
How they got in

The attacker had a contractor's password and spammed multi-factor authentication (MFA) push requests. Then they contacted the contractor on WhatsApp, posing as Uber IT. They kept going until the contractor approved one.
Going deeper

Inside, the attacker found a PowerShell script on a network share. It held hard-coded admin credentials, written straight into the script, for Uber's privileged access management system. That unlocked much more.
Lesson: stronger MFA
Use phishing-resistant MFA, or at least number matching. With number matching, you type a number from the login screen into your phone. A tired tap on a spammed prompt isn't enough.
Lesson: no secrets in scripts
Never hard-code secrets in scripts. Store them in a secrets manager instead. At Uber, one script's admin credentials unlocked much more access.
Lesson: IT won't pressure you
Teach staff that real IT won't pressure them to approve prompts. At Uber, an attacker posing as IT on WhatsApp got a prompt approved.
decks.maps: A07 Authentication Failures · secrets management

q.q: What turned one approved MFA prompt into broad access at Uber?
o: Admin credentials hard-coded in a script
A zero-day flaw in the Slack app
An unpatched virtual private network (VPN)
q.w: Admin credentials hard-coded in a script. Secrets left in plain text let the attacker escalate quickly, so they belong in a secrets manager. Not a Slack flaw or a VPN: the script's credentials unlocked the extra access.

decks.entry: A contractor's stolen password plus MFA push spam until the contractor approved one.
decks.impact: Broad access to internal chat, cloud consoles and security tools.
decks.lesson: Use number matching or phishing-resistant MFA, and never hard-code admin credentials in scripts.

attack: T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
decks.title: Capital One
cards: Key terms

Server-side request forgery (SSRF): tricking a server into fetching a URL for the attacker, often an internal one.
Cloud metadata service: a built-in cloud service that gives a server its settings and temporary credentials.
Least privilege: giving each person and process only the access their job needs, for only as long as they need it.
What happened
In 2019, a former Amazon Web Services (AWS) engineer copied data from Capital One's AWS environment. The data covered about 100 million people in the US and 6 million in Canada.
How they got in
A misconfigured web application firewall was vulnerable to server-side request forgery (SSRF). The attacker made it request the cloud metadata service. The service returned temporary credentials.
Impact
Those credentials had broad access to storage buckets. A US regulator later fined Capital One US$80 million. Capital One also settled a class action.
Lesson: SSRF is access control
SSRF is now part of A01 Broken Access Control. That category is in the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 list of web app risks.
Lesson: lock down metadata
Require Instance Metadata Service version 2 (IMDSv2) on AWS. It needs a session token first, which blocks most SSRF requests. Block metadata access from apps that don't need it.
Lesson: least privilege roles
Give cloud roles least privilege, meaning only the access their job needs. At Capital One, broad bucket access let stolen credentials reach data on millions of people.
decks.maps: A01 Broken Access Control (SSRF) · least privilege

q.q: What did the SSRF flaw let the attacker obtain at Capital One?
o: Temporary cloud credentials
The chief executive's password
The firewall's source code
q.w: Temporary cloud credentials. The server fetched its own credentials from the metadata service for the attacker, and over-broad permissions did the rest. Not a password or source code: the attacker used the server's own credentials.

decks.entry: SSRF through a misconfigured web application firewall reached the EC2 metadata service.
decks.impact: Data on about 100 million people in the US and 6 million in Canada was copied.
decks.lesson: Enforce IMDSv2 and give every role least privilege.
decks.source: Capital One and US OCC, 2019 to 2020

decks.title: Patch applications
cards: What it is

Patch applications such as browsers, Office, PDF readers and internet-facing services. Remove any that the vendor no longer supports. This is one of the eight mitigation strategies in the Essential Eight, from the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD).
Why it matters

Attackers routinely exploit known flaws, often within days of a fix coming out. So for internet-facing services, the Essential Eight sets a 48-hour deadline. It applies when the vendor rates a flaw critical or a working exploit exists.

q.q: Which application should be removed rather than patched?
o: One the vendor no longer supports
A browser with a pending update
An Office version released this year
q.w: One the vendor no longer supports. Unsupported software gets no fixes, so remove or replace it. Not the browser or the new Office version: both still get fixes, so patch them.

decks.title: Patch operating systems
cards: Key terms

Patch: an update that fixes a flaw in software.
End of support: when a vendor stops releasing security updates for a product.
What it is

Patch the operating systems (OS) on workstations, servers and network devices. Replace any operating system that is out of support. Patching the OS closes holes that let malware spread and gain more privileges.
Windows 10 is out of support
Windows 10 reached end of support in October 2025. That means it no longer gets regular security updates.
WannaCry and unpatched PCs
WannaCry in 2017 spread through unpatched Windows machines. It hit about two months after the fix was out.

q.q: A clinic still runs Windows 10 PCs with no extended support. What does the Essential Eight say to do?
o: Patch it once a year
Replace or upgrade Windows 10
Keep it if antivirus is installed
q.w: Replace or upgrade Windows 10. Out-of-support systems stop getting fixes, and upgrading them is part of patching operating systems. Not yearly patching: no new patches are coming. Not antivirus: it doesn't fix the holes.

decks.title: Multi-factor authentication
cards: What it is

Require multi-factor authentication (MFA) for remote access, privileged users and online services that hold important data. MFA means proving who you are in two different ways. It stops a stolen password being enough on its own.
Maturity matters

From Maturity Level Two, the Essential Eight expects phishing-resistant MFA, such as passkeys or FIDO2 security keys. This kind of MFA still protects you on a fake website. Text message (SMS) or app codes aren't enough, because a fake login page can relay them.

q.q: Which incidents in this app would MFA on remote access most directly have stopped?
o: Medibank and Change Healthcare
Log4Shell and the CrowdStrike outage
xz utils and MOVEit
q.w: Medibank and Change Healthcare. Both started with stolen credentials on remote access with no second factor. Not the others: Log4Shell and MOVEit were software flaws, xz utils was a backdoor, and CrowdStrike was a faulty update.

decks.title: Restrict administrative privileges
cards: What it is
Give admin rights only to people who need them, and review those rights regularly. Admins should use a separate account for admin work. Privileged accounts shouldn't browse the web or read email.
Why it matters
Attackers look for admin credentials because they give access to everything. If admins read email with a standard account, one phishing click doesn't give an attacker the whole domain.

q.q: An IT admin reads email and browses the web while logged in with their domain admin account. What's the fix?
o: Antivirus on the admin's computer
A standard account for email and web
A longer, more complex admin password
q.w: A standard account for email and web. Most attacks start there, so keep privileged accounts away from them. Not antivirus or a longer password: one phishing click could still give an attacker admin rights.

decks.title: Application control
cards: What it is
With application control, only approved programs, scripts and installers can run. Everything else is blocked by default. It's an allow-list for software: a list of the only things allowed.
Where to start
Start by blocking programs from running in places users can write to. These include Downloads, the Desktop and temporary folders. That's where malicious attachments and downloads land.

q.q: A user downloads `invoice.exe` to their Downloads folder and double-clicks it. With application control, what happens?
o: It runs, but without admin rights
It's blocked, as it isn't approved
It runs, because the user opened it
q.w: It's blocked, as it isn't approved. Allow-listing blocks anything that isn't approved, however convincing the file name is. Not either "it runs" option: the user's choice and their rights don't matter if the file isn't on the list.

decks.title: Restrict Microsoft Office macros
cards: What it is

Turn off Office macros for users who don't need them. A macro is a small program saved inside a document. Block macros in files that came from the internet. Macro-enabled documents are a classic way to deliver malware.
Real world

For years, emailed Word and Excel files asked users to “enable content”. That ran a macro that downloaded malware. Microsoft now blocks macros in internet files by default. You still need to check the settings.

q.q: Which macros should be blocked first?
o: Macros in files from the internet
Signed macros from your finance team
Macros in files on your own file server
q.w: Macros in files from the internet. They're the delivery route attackers use. Not the other two: they come from inside your organisation, and trusted, signed business macros can be allowed.

decks.title: User application hardening
cards: What it is

User application hardening means locking down everyday apps so they're harder to abuse. For example, browsers block web ads and Java from the internet. Old software, such as Internet Explorer 11, is disabled or removed.
Why it matters

Attackers abuse features, not just bugs. For example, you can stop Office from launching child processes, which are programs started by another program. That breaks a common attack where a document starts PowerShell.

q.q: Which is an example of user application hardening?
o: Backing up user files
Patching the operating system
Blocking Office child processes
q.w: Blocking Office child processes. Removing risky features from everyday apps shrinks what an attacker can use. Not backups or operating system patching: they're separate Essential Eight strategies.

decks.title: Regular backups
cards: What it is

Back up important data, software and settings regularly. Keep backups for as long as the business needs them, and test that you can restore them. Standard users shouldn't be able to change or delete backups.
Backups don't stop data theft

Backups restore data that ransomware encrypted, so you can get running again. Ransomware is malware that locks or steals data and demands payment. Backups do nothing about data that has already been stolen. So they're one layer, not the whole answer.

q.q: Why should ordinary user accounts be unable to delete backups?
o: It stops users wasting backup storage
It stops users restoring the wrong version
Malware could delete them with their rights
q.w: Malware could delete them with their rights. Malware acts with the user's rights, so backups it can't reach are backups that survive. Not storage or wrong restores: the protection is about stopping attackers, not user mistakes.

decks.title: Maturity levels
cards: Key terms

Essential Eight: eight mitigation strategies from the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) that form a security baseline.
Maturity level: one of four levels, from zero to three, each designed to resist more capable attackers.
Baseline: a minimum set of security controls to build on.
What they are

The Essential Eight has maturity levels from zero to three. Each level is designed to resist more capable attackers. Level One resists opportunistic attackers, and Level Three resists adaptive, targeted ones.
How to use them
Aim for the same maturity level across all eight strategies before moving up. A strong score on one strategy doesn't make up for a gap in another.
Know its limits

The Essential Eight is a baseline designed for internet-connected Windows networks. It's not a complete security programme. In October 2026, ASD began replacing it with ASD Essentials. For now, the current Essential Eight still applies.
It's in Australian job ads
Australian job ads often ask for the Essential Eight. Be ready to explain the eight strategies and where they stop.

q.q: What's the recommended way to improve Essential Eight maturity?
o: Get one strategy to Level Three first
Aim straight for Level Three everywhere
Raise all eight together, level by level
q.w: Raise all eight together, level by level. The strategies work together, and an attacker will use whichever one is weakest. Not one strategy first or straight to Level Three: both leave some strategies weaker than others.

decks.title: Shared responsibility
cards: What it is

The shared responsibility model splits security duties between a cloud provider and its customers. The provider secures the cloud itself: data centres, hardware and the hypervisor. You secure what you put in it: data, identities, network rules and configuration.
It shifts by service

With infrastructure as a service (IaaS), such as virtual machines, you patch the operating system. With software as a service (SaaS), you mostly manage users, data and settings. Either way, your data and who can access it are always yours.

q.q: A company leaves a storage bucket public. Whose responsibility is that?
o: Both, equally
The customer's
The cloud provider's
q.w: The customer's. Configuration is the customer's side of the shared responsibility model. Providers give you the controls, and you have to use them. Not the provider or both: the provider secures the cloud itself, not your settings.

decks.title: Identity is the perimeter
cards: Key terms

Identity and Access Management (IAM) role: a cloud identity with set permissions that trusted users or services can temporarily take on.
Least privilege: giving each person and process only the access their job needs, for only as long as they need it.
AWS root user: the login that created an Amazon Web Services (AWS) account, with full control over it.
What it is
In the cloud, identity and access management (IAM) decides what every person and service can do. A leaked key with broad rights is as bad as an open firewall.
Protect the top accounts
Protect the Amazon Web Services (AWS) root user or the Microsoft Entra ID Global Administrator with multi-factor authentication (MFA). Use these accounts rarely.
Limit roles and credentials
Give people and apps roles with least privilege, meaning only the access their job needs. Prefer short-lived credentials over long-lived access keys. Review permissions regularly.

q.q: Which is safest for an app running on an AWS server that needs to read one bucket?
o: An IAM role allowing read access to that bucket only
An access key with admin rights saved in the code
The root user's credentials
q.w: An IAM role allowing read access to that bucket only. Roles give temporary credentials automatically, and least privilege limits what a compromise can reach. Not an admin key or root credentials: if leaked, they give access to the whole account.

decks.title: Cloud logging
cards: Key terms

AWS CloudTrail: an Amazon Web Services (AWS) service that records API calls and console sign-ins.
Application programming interface (API): a way for programs to ask another system for data over a network.
Trail: a CloudTrail setting that copies events to storage you choose.
What to turn on

Amazon Web Services (AWS) CloudTrail records application programming interface (API) calls and console sign-ins. In Microsoft's cloud, Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs and the Azure Activity log do similar jobs.
Keep logs beyond 90 days
CloudTrail's event history only keeps 90 days. So send a trail to protected storage, ideally in a separate logging account.
What to alert on

Attackers often disable logging first, so alert on that above all. Also alert on root or Global Administrator sign-ins, sign-ins without multi-factor authentication (MFA), new access keys and permission changes.

q.q: Someone stops CloudTrail logging in your AWS account at 2am. What should happen?
o: Nothing, as logging is optional
A ticket to review on the next workday
An alert, treated as a possible intrusion
q.w: An alert, treated as a possible intrusion. Disabling logs is a classic attacker move to hide what comes next. Not a ticket for later: the attacker gets hours unseen. Not nothing: logs are your record of what happened.

decks.title: Public storage
cards: The risk
Cloud storage buckets and blobs left open to the public are behind many data exposures. It's a configuration problem: A02 Security Misconfiguration in the OWASP Top 10:2025.
The controls

On Amazon Web Services (AWS), S3 Block Public Access has been on by default for new buckets since April 2023. You can also enforce it across the account. Check older buckets, bucket policies and sharing links. Scan for public access automatically.

q.q: A bucket created in 2021 holds customer files. What's the first check?
o: Its file naming scheme
Its storage class settings
Its public access settings
q.w: Its public access settings, including the bucket policy. Older buckets predate the safer defaults, so confirm public access is blocked. Not storage class or file names: neither controls who can read the files.

decks.title: The metadata service
cards: Key terms

Cloud metadata service: a built-in cloud service that gives a server its settings and temporary credentials.
Server-side request forgery (SSRF): tricking a server into fetching a URL for the attacker, often an internal one.
Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2): the AWS metadata service version that needs a session token first.
What it is

Cloud servers can query a local metadata service for details, including temporary credentials for their role. On Amazon Web Services (AWS), it's at 169.254.169.254. It's useful for apps, and a prize for attackers.
Protect it: require IMDSv2
On AWS, require Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2). It needs a session token, which makes simple server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks far harder.
Least privilege limits damage
Give server roles least privilege, meaning only the access their job needs. Then stolen credentials can't reach much. Capital One in 2019 shows what goes wrong.

q.q: Why does requiring IMDSv2 help against SSRF?
o: It needs a session token first
It encrypts metadata responses
It blocks outbound web traffic
q.w: It needs a session token first. Getting the token takes a PUT request, and most SSRF flaws can only make simple GET requests. Not encryption or blocking traffic: IMDSv2 doesn't do either.

decks.title: Notifiable Data Breaches scheme
cards: Key terms

Notifiable Data Breaches scheme: Australia's rules for reporting serious data breaches, under the Privacy Act 1988.
Eligible data breach: a breach of personal information likely to cause serious harm that you can't prevent.
Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC): Australia's privacy regulator.
What it is
Under Australia's Privacy Act 1988, covered organisations must report an eligible data breach to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC). They must also tell the people affected.
Who it covers
The Notifiable Data Breaches scheme mostly covers businesses with turnover over A$3 million. It also covers all health service providers and some others.
When a breach is eligible

A data breach is eligible when three things are true. First, personal information is accessed or disclosed without authorisation, or lost in a way that makes that likely. Second, it's likely to cause serious harm. Third, you can't prevent that harm.
How fast to act
If you only suspect an eligible data breach, you have 30 days to assess it. If it is eligible, you notify as soon as practicable.

q.q: You suspect an eligible data breach but aren't sure. How long do you have to assess it?
o: 72 hours
30 days
One year
q.w: 30 days. The scheme expects a reasonable, quick assessment within 30 days, then notification as soon as practicable if it's eligible. 72 hours is the trap answer: that's the ransomware payment deadline. One year is far too slow.

decks.title: NZ Privacy Act 2020
cards: Key terms

Notifiable privacy breach: a privacy breach that has caused, or is likely to cause, serious harm.
Privacy Commissioner: New Zealand's privacy regulator.
What it is
In New Zealand, a privacy breach that has caused or is likely to cause serious harm is a notifiable privacy breach. You must tell the Privacy Commissioner and affected people as soon as practicable.
The penalty
Failing to notify the Privacy Commissioner of a notifiable privacy breach is an offence. The fine is up to NZ$10,000.
Why speed matters
Quick notice of a privacy breach lets people protect themselves, for example by watching for scams. That matters even more than the fine.

q.q: Under the NZ Privacy Act 2020, who must be told about a notifiable privacy breach?
o: The Privacy Commissioner only
Affected people and the NZ Police
The Commissioner and affected people
q.w: The Commissioner and affected people. Both the regulator and the people affected need to know, as soon as practicable. Not the Commissioner only: affected people need to protect themselves. Not the police: the Act names the Commissioner instead.

decks.title: Reporting ransomware payments
cards: Key terms

Ransomware: malware that locks or steals data and demands payment.
Cyber extortion: demanding payment to stop an attack or keep stolen data private.
Sanction: a government ban on a person or group, such as freezing their money or banning travel.
What it is

Under Australia's Cyber Security Act 2024, some businesses must report a ransomware or cyber extortion payment. They report it to the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) within 72 hours of paying. The rule started on 30 May 2025.
Who must report
Businesses with an annual turnover over A$3 million must report a ransomware or cyber extortion payment. Critical infrastructure entities must report regardless of turnover.
Reporting isn't approval
Reporting a ransomware payment isn't approval. Paying is legal but discouraged. Paying a sanctioned group can break sanctions law.
One incident, several reports
One incident can trigger several separate reports. They cover privacy, the ransom payment and the cyber incident itself.

q.q: An Australian company with A$50 million turnover pays a ransom. What must it do?
o: Nothing, payments are private
Report the payment to ASD within 72 hours
Report it at the end of the financial year
q.w: Report the payment to ASD within 72 hours. The Cyber Security Act 2024 requires this for businesses over the A$3 million threshold. Not nothing: the payment must be reported. Not year end: the deadline is 72 hours.

decks.title: Who to call
cards: Australia

In Australia, report cyber incidents to the Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre. Use ReportCyber at cyber.gov.au. Report privacy breaches to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC).
New Zealand

In New Zealand, report cyber incidents to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC). It began absorbing CERT NZ in 2023 and has since retired the CERT NZ brand. Report privacy breaches to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner.

q.q: In New Zealand, which agency has taken over CERT NZ's role for cyber incident reports?
o: The New Zealand Police
The National Cyber Security Centre
The Office of the Privacy Commissioner
q.w: The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC). CERT NZ has been merged into the NCSC, a process that began in 2023. Not the Privacy Commissioner: privacy breaches still go there, but cyber incidents don't. Not the police: they didn't take over CERT NZ's role.

decks.title: MITRE ATT&CK in two minutes
cards: Key terms

MITRE ATT&CK: a free catalogue of real attacker behaviour.
Tactic: an attacker's goal, such as Initial Access.
Technique: a way attackers reach a goal, with an ID such as T1110.
Sub-technique: a more specific version of a technique, such as T1110.003.
Tactics are the attacker's goals

MITRE ATT&CK is a free catalogue of real attacker behaviour. Its tactics are the attacker's goals. Since v19 (April 2026), the Enterprise matrix has 15 tactics. They include Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Stealth, Credential Access, Lateral Movement and Exfiltration.
Techniques are how attackers act
Each ATT&CK tactic holds techniques with IDs, like T1110 Brute Force. Sub-techniques add a number: T1110.003 is Password Spraying. One technique can sit under several tactics.
IDs give everyone one name
Security operations centre (SOC) tickets, threat reports and detection rules all use ATT&CK IDs. They act as a shared language, so everyone uses the same name for the same behaviour.

q.q: In ATT&CK, what does T1110.003 identify?
o: A Windows event ID
A sub-technique: password spraying
A Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) ID
q.w: A sub-technique: password spraying. T numbers are ATT&CK techniques, and the .003 marks a sub-technique of T1110 Brute Force. Not a CVE ID or a Windows event ID: those name software flaws and log events, not attacker behaviour.

decks.title: Many users, one source
cards: The evidence

This is a Windows server's Security log over two minutes, all network logons. Forty different users each have one failed logon from the same public address. Then one logon succeeds. Event ID 4625 is a failed logon, and 4624 is a successful one.

o: Password spraying, one success
A backup job checking each account
One user retrying a forgotten password
qs.w: Password spraying, with one success for dlee. Trying one password per user from one source avoids lockouts, and the final 4624 means a guess worked. A forgotten password or backup job wouldn't hit forty accounts. A public address reaching this server directly is a finding too.

o: Delete the event logs
Email all forty users to ask if it was them
Reset dlee's password and revoke their sessions
qs.w: Reset dlee's password and revoke their sessions. Contain the compromised account first. Then block the source, review what the account did and start a timeline as you escalate. Not deleting logs: that destroys evidence. Not emailing all forty users: it delays containing the one breached account.

after: In Microsoft Sentinel, this Kusto Query Language (KQL) query finds sources that failed against many accounts in ten minutes.

SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize users = dcount(TargetUserName) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where users > 10

decks.title: A noisy SSH server
cards: The evidence
This is a Linux server's Secure Shell (SSH) log, simplified. It shows about 300 failed logins in five minutes from one address. No successful logins appear.

Failed password  root
  from 198.51.100.23
Failed password  root
  from 198.51.100.23
Failed password  admin (invalid)
  from 198.51.100.23
...  about 300 in 5 minutes

o: A routine software update
Brute force, with no success seen
A successful compromise of the server
qs.w: Brute force, with no success seen. Brute force means guessing passwords again and again until one works. Here, one source made hundreds of failed attempts on common usernames. Nothing shows it worked, but you still check. Not a compromise: no login succeeded. Not an update: updates don't cause failed logins.

qs.q: Before closing this alert, what do you check?
o: The server's CPU temperature
Whether the address is in Australia
Any “Accepted” login from that address
qs.w: Any “Accepted” login from that address. You need to confirm the attacker never got in. Then harden SSH with key-only logins, no root login, and rate limiting or fail2ban, a tool that blocks repeat offenders. Location and temperature don't show whether a login worked.

after: On the server, search for any successful login from the attacking address. On Red Hat or Fedora, the service unit is called sshd, not ssh.

decks.title: A reported email
cards: The evidence

A user reports this email and hasn't clicked the link. Its three email checks are Sender Policy Framework (SPF), DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC). Together, they show whether an email really came from the domain it claims.

From: "Microsoft 365"
  no-reply@micros0ft-support.example
Reply-To: helpdesk@freemail.example
Subject: Your password expires today
SPF fail · DKIM none · DMARC fail
Link: login.micros0ft-support.example

o: A delivery receipt
Credential phishing
A real Microsoft notice
qs.w: Credential phishing, which tries to steal login details. The signs are a look-alike domain, failed SPF and DMARC, urgency and a login link. Not a real Microsoft notice: the sender's domain only imitates Microsoft's. Not a delivery receipt: it asks you to log in.

o: Reply to the sender to complain
Remove all copies and check who clicked
Forward it to all staff as a warning, link included
qs.w: Remove all copies and check who clicked. Others probably got it too, so remove every copy and block the domain. Then check proxy or sign-in logs for anyone who clicked or entered a password. Replying protects nobody, and forwarding the link spreads the risk.

after: The user did exactly the right thing. A quick thank-you makes them more likely to report the next one. That's how many phishing campaigns get caught early.

decks.title: A root sign-in
cards: The evidence

These are key fields from an Amazon Web Services (AWS) CloudTrail event at 3am. CloudTrail records sign-ins and other actions in an AWS account. Nobody on the team uses the root user. MFAUsed shows whether multi-factor authentication (MFA) was used.

eventName: ConsoleLogin
userIdentity.type: Root
sourceIPAddress: 192.0.2.77
MFAUsed: No
ConsoleLogin: Success

o: A routine automated backup
A failed root sign-in attempt
A successful root sign-in, no MFA
qs.w: A successful root sign-in with no MFA. ConsoleLogin Success, Root and MFAUsed No should never happen unannounced. Not a failed attempt: the result is Success. Not a backup: ConsoleLogin records a sign-in, not a backup job.

o: Wait to see if it happens again
Treat it as a compromise and secure root
Delete the CloudTrail event to clear the alert
qs.w: Treat it as a compromise and secure root. Change the root password and add MFA. Then hunt for new users, access keys and changed permissions since the sign-in. Waiting gives the attacker more time. Deleting the event destroys evidence and doesn't remove the attacker.

after: Protect the root user with phishing-resistant MFA, which still protects you on a fake website. Remove any root access keys, and alert on every root sign-in. Day-to-day work should use roles, never root.

attack: T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
decks.title: Word starts PowerShell
cards: The evidence
This is an endpoint alert from a finance laptop, with file paths shortened. WINWORD.EXE is Microsoft Word. PowerShell is Microsoft's command-line shell and scripting language.

Parent:  …\Office16\WINWORD.EXE
Process: …\powershell.exe
Command: powershell -nop -w hidden
  -enc SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0A…

o: Word is checking for software updates
The user is writing a PowerShell script
A malicious document ran hidden PowerShell
qs.w: A malicious document ran hidden PowerShell. Word as the parent process, a hidden window and an encoded command are classic signs of a malicious macro. A macro is a small program saved inside a document. Updates and hand-written scripts don't usually look like this.

o: Switch it off at the wall straight away
Isolate it from the network, but keep it on
Delete the Word document from the laptop
qs.w: Isolate it from the network, but keep it on. Isolation stops the spread, and keeping it on preserves evidence in memory. Then find the document, its sender and other recipients. Switching off loses memory evidence. Deleting the document doesn't stop code that already ran.

after: In Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, this Kusto Query Language (KQL) query finds Office apps starting PowerShell.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe", "excel.exe")
| where FileName =~ "powershell.exe"

decks.title: Qubole cross-account trust abuse
cards: Key terms

Identity and Access Management (IAM) role: a cloud identity with set permissions that trusted users or services can temporarily take on.
Trust policy: the part of an IAM role that says who is allowed to take it on.
Third-party access: access to your systems or data held by an outside company, such as a vendor.
What happened

From 14 to 26 October 2026, an attacker got into the Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts of many Qubole customers. The attacker used credentials tied to a Qubole AWS account. Wiz published the findings on 9 November 2026, working with Sentra and Mandiant.
How they got in

Customers had created Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles that trusted Qubole's AWS account. That let Qubole's data platform reach their data. The attacker took over two Qubole IAM users and assumed those roles. In many cases, the roles were left over from integrations the customer no longer used.
Impact

The attacker read secrets from Secrets Manager, AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Parameter Store and Lambda environment variables. Then it tested the keys it found. It also copied S3 data, sometimes whole buckets. SecurityWeek reports more than a dozen organisations were hit.
Lesson: remove old vendor roles
Remove vendor roles you no longer use. In many cases, the abused roles were left over from integrations the customer no longer used.
Lesson: tighten role trust

Trust the vendor's exact IAM role, not their whole account (`:root`). If the vendor publishes fixed IP addresses, allow only those. An External ID is a code the vendor sends when taking on your role. It isn't a secret.
Lesson: log S3 data events
Turn on S3 data events, logs of who read each file, for sensitive buckets. Some victims had no S3 data events or access logs. They couldn't tell which files were read.
decks.maps: A01 Broken Access Control · A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) GV.SC supply chain risk

q.q: Why did the attacker's requests into customer AWS accounts succeed?
o: The customers' roles still trusted Qubole's AWS account
The customers' S3 buckets were set to allow public reads
AWS had an unpatched flaw in its IAM service
q.w: The customers' roles still trusted Qubole's AWS account. Old trust policies let anyone holding Qubole-side credentials assume the roles. Not public buckets: the attacker got in through the roles. Not an AWS flaw: none was needed.

decks.entry: Two hijacked Qubole IAM users took on old customer roles that trusted Qubole.
decks.impact: The attacker read secrets and S3 data at more than a dozen customers.
decks.lesson: Delete unused vendor roles. Trust exact roles, not whole accounts.

decks.title: SSHole: OpenSSH password bypass
cards: Key terms

musl: a small C library, the basic code programs rely on, used by Alpine Linux instead of the more common glibc.
Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM): a Linux system that handles how users log in and how their passwords are checked.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE): an ID that names one publicly known vulnerability.
Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue: a US government list of flaws that attackers are exploiting in the wild.
What happened

On 5 November 2026, OpenSSH released 10.6p2 to fix CVE-2026-123158, nicknamed "SSHole". On 9 November, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue.
How they got in

A very long password could get through Secure Shell (SSH) password login on some Linux systems. It needed the musl C library and an OpenSSH built without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM). Alpine Linux is the main example. glibc distros like Debian and Ubuntu aren't affected.
Why the password matched
It only worked on accounts locked with `*` in the password file, such as key-only accounts. musl returned `*` for the over-long password, which matched.
Impact

Exploitation started fast. SANS Internet Storm Center honeypots, decoy systems that attract attackers, saw attempts on 5 November, the day public exploit code appeared. BleepingComputer and GreyNoise report break-ins within days. The flaw scores 8.1 (High) on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 3.1.
Lesson: patch KEV flaws fast
Patch internet-facing SSH fast once a flaw hits the KEV list. With SSHole, attackers reportedly broke in within days.
Lesson: use key-based logins
Use key-based logins and set `PasswordAuthentication no`. Key-only logins block this bypass.
Lesson: know where Alpine runs
Know which of your hosts and containers run Alpine. That decides whether you're exposed.
decks.maps: A07 Authentication Failures · NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) ID.RA risk assessment and PR.PS patching

q.q: Which servers were exposed to SSHole?
o: Alpine and other musl builds without PAM
Ubuntu and Debian servers with password logins
Servers that allow SSH key logins only
q.w: Alpine and other musl builds without PAM. The bug also needs password logins turned on and an account locked with `*`. Not Ubuntu or Debian: glibc distros weren't affected. Not key-only servers: key-only logins block the bypass.

decks.entry: An over-long password got past SSH login on musl builds without PAM.
decks.impact: Attackers broke in within days. CISA listed it as known exploited on 9 November.
decks.lesson: Use key-based SSH logins and patch known exploited flaws fast.

decks.title: Amadeus booking breach
cards: Key terms

Third-party access: access to your systems or data held by an outside company, such as a vendor.
System account: an account that software or a system uses to log in, instead of a person.
Least privilege: giving each person and process only the access their job needs, for only as long as they need it.
What happened

In late October 2026, Cathay Pacific said Amadeus had told it about unauthorised access to booking data. Amadeus is a travel technology provider. In early November, Qantas said Amadeus had told it the same. Cathay says the access ran from August 2023 to September 2026.
How they got in

Amadeus says a vulnerability in a booking-display environment made certain booking data accessible. Cathay Pacific says Amadeus told it the attacker used login credentials assigned to a system account. A system account is one that software uses, not a person. Neither company has published full technical details.
Impact

Cathay Pacific says about 53,000 bookings were affected, with no evidence that payment or financial data was accessed. Japan Airlines and its subsidiary reported about 92,000 affected customers, and ANA, Asiana and Korean Air were also hit. Qantas says its own systems weren't affected, but it doesn't yet know which of its customers, if any, had data accessed.
Lesson: suppliers hold your data
Your customers' data is only as safe as your supplier's systems. Qantas says its own systems weren't affected, yet its customers may still be exposed through Amadeus.
Lesson: guard system accounts
Give service and system accounts the same care as human ones. Use strong secrets, rotate them, monitor them and apply least privilege.
Lesson: spot long-running access
Access that lasted about three years before it was found points to a monitoring gap. Continuous monitoring helps you notice unusual account use sooner.
decks.maps: CSF GV.SC supply chain · CSF DE.CM continuous monitoring

q.q: Qantas says its own systems weren't touched. Why might its customers still be affected?
o: Their booking data was held in a supplier's system
Qantas staff reused passwords on the booking portal
Customers clicked a phishing link sent by the attackers
q.w: Their booking data was held in a supplier's system. Your data can leak from someone else's network; only Amadeus was reported as accessed. Not reused passwords or phishing: neither was reported here.

decks.entry: Amadeus cites a flaw. Cathay says a system account's login was used.
decks.impact: About 53,000 Cathay Pacific bookings and about 92,000 customers of Japan Airlines and its subsidiary. ANA, Asiana and Korean Air were also hit, and Qantas was notified.
decks.lesson: Your customers' data is only as safe as your suppliers' systems.
decks.source: Cathay Pacific, Qantas and Japan Airlines statements, 2026

decks.title: Maersk legacy system breach
cards: Key terms

Legacy system: an old system that is still running, often no longer updated or watched closely.
Asset inventory: a list of every system and device an organisation owns.
Ransomware: malware that locks or steals data and demands payment.
Leak site: a website where a ransomware gang names victims and posts stolen data to pressure them.
What happened

On 11 November 2026, shipping company Maersk confirmed that someone accessed a local legacy system and took data from it. A legacy system is an old one that is still running. Maersk inherited this one through an earlier acquisition.
How they got in
Not disclosed. Maersk hasn't said how the attackers got in or when the intrusion began. Some reporting links the data to LF Logistics, which Maersk bought in 2022. Maersk hasn't confirmed this.
The ransomware claim
Separately, the WhiteArmor ransomware gang listed Maersk on its leak site. WhiteArmor says it holds about 100 GB of data and wants US$5 million. Maersk hasn't linked the claim to the breach.
What Maersk says
Maersk says the incident is isolated. Its early findings suggest no sensitive data was disclosed. It found no sign that other systems or shipping operations were affected.
Lesson: you inherit their risk
When you acquire a company, you also acquire its old servers and their risk.
Lesson: list, then fix or retire
Put inherited systems in your asset inventory, your list of every system you own. Then patch, isolate or retire them.
Lesson: watch what you inherit
A system you forgot about is one you aren't monitoring. Add every inherited system to your monitoring.
decks.maps: CSF ID.AM asset management · CSF GV.SC supply chain

q.q: Why are systems like the one breached at Maersk often higher risk?
o: They often miss normal patching and monitoring
They usually run in a less secure public cloud
They are usually the company's newest systems
q.w: They often miss normal patching and monitoring. Inherited legacy systems often sit outside your inventory. Not the public cloud: this was a local system. Not the newest: legacy systems are old ones.

decks.entry: Not disclosed. A legacy system inherited through an acquisition was accessed.
decks.impact: A ransomware gang claims about 100 GB of data. Maersk says the incident is isolated.
